title: Memory in Foundry
summary: Foundry memory (preview) is managed long-term memory: an LLM extracts facts from conversations, consolidates them into a memory store and retrieves them across sessions, scoped per user.
useIf: An agent should remember user preferences, past issues or learned routines across sessions.
avoidIf: The content is shared policy or documents, the project needs VNet integration for memory stores, or preview is not allowed.

explain.md: Foundry memory is designed for **long-term** memory: knowledge retained across sessions. Short-term memory is the current session's conversation and is handled by the orchestration framework [[r7]]. Memories live as items in a managed **memory store**. The system works in three phases: **extraction** (pull preferences, facts and context from a conversation), **consolidation** (an LLM merges duplicates and resolves conflicts, such as a new allergy), and **retrieval** (search the store for relevant memories) [[r7]].

explain.title: Memory phases
explain.alt: Conversation text is extracted into candidate memories, consolidated by an LLM into the store, and retrieved into later sessions.

flowchart LR

explain.md: You use memory in two ways: attach the **memory search tool** to a prompt agent so it reads and writes during conversations, or call the **memory store APIs** for direct control over items, retention and lifecycle [[r7]]. Controls include item-level create, read, update, list and delete, a store-level default TTL set at creation, and direct remember-or-forget commands [[r7]]. Low-level APIs need an explicit `scope` on every request, and automatic scope resolution from the caller's identity works only with the memory search tool and `scope` set to `{{$userId}}` [[r7]].

explain.title: Preview, checked 2026-10-13
explain.md: Memory and the Memory Store API are preview, with no SLA. Memory needs compatible Azure OpenAI chat and embedding deployments. **VNet integration is not supported for memory stores.** Because an LLM extracts and consolidates memories, prompt injection and memory corruption are risks: use Content Safety prompt injection detection and adversarial testing [[r7]].

whereToUse: Support or shopping agents that should recall a user's preferences and past issues
Planning agents that reuse stable constraints such as seat or dietary preferences
Agents that learn recurring workflows (procedural memory) for a given user
Any agent where a user may ask to remember or forget something explicitly

use: Facts are user-specific, learned over time and should persist across sessions
You want extraction and conflict resolution done for you
You need item-level delete and TTL for privacy and retention
avoid: Shared policy or curated documents: use a Foundry IQ knowledge base. Memory is per-user and LLM-consolidated (inference)
User-provided documents in a chat: use file search
Networks that require VNet integration for the store, or policies that forbid preview
flips: Memory must be auditable and deterministic: store structured facts yourself and keep LLM extraction out
Volume exceeds 10,000 memories per scope: shard scopes or prune with TTL
A regulator needs proof of deletion: use item-level delete and log the deletion

pitfalls.symptom: One user's memories surface for another user
pitfalls.cause: Low-level API calls used the wrong or a shared `scope`
pitfalls.fix: Set `scope` explicitly per request, or use the memory search tool with `scope` set to `{{$userId}}` [[r7]].

pitfalls.symptom: The agent confidently repeats a wrong 'fact' about a user
pitfalls.cause: A bad statement or injected text was extracted and consolidated
pitfalls.fix: Filter inputs with prompt injection detection, review and delete items, and test adversarially [[r7]].

pitfalls.symptom: TTL or procedural memory settings cannot be changed later
pitfalls.cause: Some defaults, such as procedural memory and default TTL, are configured at store creation
pitfalls.fix: Plan them at creation and verify post-create updates in your API version [[r7]].

scenarios.title: Remember each customer across visits
scenarios.situation: A customer assistant should recall a user's preferences and the last unresolved issue the next time they return, and forget on request.
unknowns: How long may memories be kept?
scenarios.question: How do you provide continuity?

options.name: Memory store with the memory search tool, `scope` set to `{{$userId}}` and a default TTL
options.why: Managed extraction and consolidation, per-user scope and item-level delete for forget requests.
options.tradeoff: Preview, and LLM-extracted facts can be wrong.

options.name: Resend full chat history each session
options.tradeoff: Token cost grows and history from old sessions is hard to prune.

options.name: Put shared policy documents into memory
options.why: Memory is per-user and LLM-consolidated, so curated content gets rewritten and scoped wrongly.
options.tradeoff: Use a knowledge base for shared content.

flips.then: Own structured profile table with explicit writes.
Own store until memory reaches GA.

scenarios.takeaway: Memory is for user-specific facts, not shared knowledge.

scenarios.title: Isolated network project
scenarios.situation: A project runs behind private networking with VNet integration required for every data store. The agent needs per-user preference recall.
unknowns: Is a private database already approved?
scenarios.question: What do you do for memory?

options.name: Build a small preference store in a VNet-integrated database and retrieve it in code
options.why: Memory stores do not support VNet integration, so the requirement rules the managed store out.
options.tradeoff: You write extraction, retention and deletion logic.

options.name: Use Foundry memory anyway
options.why: It breaks the VNet integration requirement.
options.tradeoff: Right when the network rule does not apply.

options.name: Resend recent chat history
options.why: Works for short horizons with no store.
options.tradeoff: No long-term recall and rising token cost.

flips.if: Docs later list VNet support for memory stores
Only the agent needs private networking, not the memory store

scenarios.takeaway: Check the limitations list against your network rules before adopting a preview feature.

quiz.q: A memory store allows at most 100 scopes and 10,000 memories per scope. What is the maximum number of memories one store can hold?
quiz.explain: 100 x 10,000 = 1,000,000. This is derived from the documented quotas, which apply to the preview.

quiz.q: When does Foundry resolve `scope` automatically from the caller's identity?
options: Only with the memory search tool and `scope` set to `{{$userId}}`
quiz.explain: Low-level APIs need an explicit scope in each request. Automatic resolution is supported only for the memory search tool with `{{$userId}}`.

quiz.q: Which content belongs in a Foundry IQ knowledge base rather than in memory?
options: A summary of last week's chat
quiz.explain: Memory is for user-specific facts learned over time. Curated organization content belongs in a knowledge base. The other items match the profile, chat summary and procedural memory types.

flashcards.front: Three phases and three types of Foundry memory?
flashcards.back: Phases: extraction, consolidation, retrieval. Types: user profile, chat summary, procedural. All three types are on by default. Memory is preview.
100 scopes per store, 10,000 memories per scope, 1,000 search and 1,000 update requests per minute. No VNet integration for memory stores.
